issues.issue: The recital fixes the Building at "approximately forty-seven thousand, four hundred fifty (47,450) square feet," while Section 1.2 states the Rentable Area of the Premises is 47,480 square feet. A court could be asked whether the recital or the operative section controls the square footage on which Base Rent is computed.

"Rentable Area" is measured on "the main level of the Building," a term the Lease nowhere defines and which has no stated boundary where floor levels are split or partly mezzanine. The measurement formula (outside of exterior walls, centerline of party walls) gives no rule for outside storage or attached structures.

This section states 47,480 square feet, while the Recitals describe the Building as 47,450 square feet and the Section 4.1 rent table's annual totals compute exactly off 47,450. A court could be asked which figure governs Rentable Area of the Premises.

The remeasurement mechanism obliges the parties to "amend all relevant provisions of this Lease (including, without limitation, Base Rent)" without stating the formula or any dispute mechanism, an unenforceable agreement to agree. Which provisions are "relevant" and how Base Rent is recalculated is left open.

The flat "fifteen (15) years" cannot be squared with Section 2.2, which expires the Lease on the last day of the fifteenth Lease Year, and Section 2.4, which starts Lease Year one at the first full month after the Commencement Date, so the term can run more than fifteen years. Section 3.3's automatic extension to January 31 lengthens it further.

The Commencement Date is defined as the Delivery Date, but Section 5.1 makes delivery depend on Tenant's own delivery of insurance evidence, so the date on which the term and Tenant's insurance obligations begin is not fixed by the instrument. The cross-reference in the text is also garbled ("Section §.1").

"Last day of the fifteenth (15th) Lease Year" read with the Section 2.4 definition of Lease Year produces an expiration later than the fifteen years stated in Section 2, and the section is further made "subject to Section 3.3." A court could be asked to fix the actual expiration date.

The definition leaves the stub period between a mid-month Commencement Date and the first day of the first full month outside every Lease Year, so the term measured in Lease Years exceeds fifteen calendar years. It is ambiguous whether that partial period counts toward Lease Year one for rent-step and Percentage Rent purposes.

Renewal is conditioned on Tenant "not [being] in default," yet Section 3.2 makes the options automatically exercised with no action required by Tenant. A court would have to decide whether an uncured default defeats a renewal that occurs automatically, and at what moment default is measured.

The provision says the renewal Rent shall be "as adjusted sel forth in Section 4," but Section 4.1 fixes Base Rent only through year 30 and by formula for the second and third options. Whether "same terms and conditions" carries the Percentage Rent Threshold unchanged into renewal terms is unstated.

Automatic exercise "with no action required by Tenant" sits against the Section 3 preamble conditioning the options on Tenant not being in default. A court could be asked whether Landlord may treat a defaulting Tenant's automatic renewal as ineffective.

The automatic January 31 extension cannot be squared with Section 2.2's expiration on the last day of the fifteenth Lease Year, and it is unclear whether the extension is available after the third renewal term or only within it. The section makes automatic extension turn on a one-year advance notice of non-extension that may precede the event triggering it.

Rent is payable "without deduction or setoff for any reason whatsoever," but Section 17.2(b) expressly lets Tenant abate Base Rent, Percentage Rent and Additional Rent, and Section 4.5 grants a monthly credit against Base Rent. A court could be asked which controls.

The rent schedule's year ranges are internally incoherent as written ("4-5," "41-75," "16-20" for a fifteen-year initial term plus five-year options), leaving the years to which each rate applies uncertain. The second- and third-option CPI formulas also do not identify the index base month or how the "percentage (expressed as a fraction)" increase is measured.

The annual totals in the table are computed on 47,450 square feet, while Section 1.2 defines Rentable Area of the Premises as 47,480 square feet, and Base Rent is stated to be "based on the Rentable Area of the Premises." A court could be asked whether the stated dollar totals or the per-square-foot rate times the defined area governs.

"[A]n assignment or subleasing for a use other than a retail use such that Percentage Rent would not be applicable" gives no test for when a use ceases to be "retail," and mixed retail/non-retail subleases are unaddressed. The formula also assumes five prior Lease Years of Percentage Rent exist, which they may not.

The twelve Allocated Thresholds total only $1,300,000, one tenth of the $13,000,000 Percentage Rent Threshold they are said to allocate. A court would have to construe which figure governs a partial Lease Year or a Non-retail Transfer.

The Gross Sales exclusions end in open-ended catch-alls — "other receipts which are remitted to a governmental or other licensing entity" and "sales of items for charitable purposes" — whose scope against the enumerated specifics is contestable. It is also unclear whether internet or catalog sales merely fulfilled from the Premises are "in or from the Premises."

"[A]n underpayment of three percent (3%) or more of Percentage Rent" does not say three percent of the year audited, of the period audited, or of total rent, so the audit-cost trigger is indeterminate. The confidentiality undertaking likewise has no carve-out for disclosure to a mortgagee or purchaser, whom Section 18.1 contemplates receiving Lease information.

The disclaimer that Tenant "has made no covenant to continuously operate" cannot be squared with Section 8.2's affirmative requirement that Tenant open a Gander Mountain store within one year after the Delivery Date. A court could be asked whether any operating obligation survives.

"[A]ll amounts required to be paid by Tenant under the terms of this Lease, including Section 6" is a catch-all whose single enumerated example invites an expressio unius argument that only tax-type items are Additional Rent. Whether items such as the Section 4.4 service charge or Section 17.5 reimbursements are recoverable as Rent turns on this.

The five percent late charge is labelled "liquidated damages" while the section simultaneously recites unquantifiable actual costs, exposing the charge to construction as an unenforceable penalty. The section also refers to a ten-day grace period while stating Section 17 controls payment timing, leaving when the charge attaches contestable.

The $675,000 cap and the $8,050 "Monthly Credit" do not reconcile — twelve monthly credits per Lease Year would take roughly seven years to exhaust the cap — and "in each Lease Year" does not say how many months in a year the credit runs. Nor does the section say what happens to any unapplied balance at termination.

Tenant's acceptance of the Building "as is, with all faults and defects ... without representation or warranty" sits against Landlord's affirmative representations in Sections 19.4, 23.2 and 24.1 that the Premises comply with law and are free of Hazardous Material. A court could be asked which governs a defect existing at delivery.

"[I]n a manner consistent with a Gander Mountain prototype building" is an external, undefined and changeable standard against which Tenant's Work must be judged. The section also gives Landlord approval rights only over components "which adversely affect[] the structural integrity of the Building," a phrase with no stated threshold.

Tenant's exclusive right to "the pylon sign on the Land (as may be identified on Exhibit B)" depends on an Exhibit B site plan that is not completed in the instrument, which merely lists items "[t]o Show." A court would have to determine which pylon, if any, the grant reaches.

Installation is permitted only "at a location acceptable to Landlord and Tenant," an agreement to agree with no default location and no standard of reasonableness stated in the section. Section 25.12's general reasonableness rule applies only where consent is "required," which may not cover mutual acceptability.

The definition sweeps Landlord's contest costs into "Tax(es)" payable by Tenant, while Section 6.4 puts contests at Tenant's cost and gives Tenant the refunds. A court could be asked whether Tenant pays Landlord's contest expenses on top of the costs Section 6.4 already assigns to it.

The first sentence makes Tenant pay Taxes falling due in the term "regardless of whether such Taxes are attributable to or on account of a prior year," while the next sentence limits Tenant to "its portion of Taxes allocable to the Lease term." The provision thus contradicts itself on pre-term tax years.

Making a tax bill "at all times ... conclusive evidence of the amount of Taxes" is hard to square with Section 6.4, which gives Tenant the right to contest the amount or validity of any Tax. A court could be asked whether the conclusive-evidence clause forecloses Tenant's contest rights.

The proration rule that Taxes include only the proportion falling within the Lease term after the Rent Commencement Date cannot be squared with Section 6.2.1's "regardless of whether such Taxes are attributable to or on account of a prior year." Which rule applies to a straddling fiscal year is left open.

"[A]ny other tax, assessment, charge or levy upon the Rent" is a general catch-all following a list of Landlord-specific transfer and income taxes, and it collides with the following sentence's substitute-tax obligation measured by "gross receipts from real estate." Which sentence captures a gross-receipts or rent tax is contestable.

The last sentence — Tenant pays additional Taxes if the contest "was initiated by Landlord solely at Tenant's request or initiated by Tenant independently" — leaves unaddressed who bears additional Taxes from a contest Landlord initiates on its own. "[R]equest that the Landlord contest" also imposes no stated duty on Landlord to do so.

The warranty that taxes "assessed and due ... and not delinquent have been paid" is self-cancelling as drafted: taxes that have been paid are neither due nor delinquent. What it warrants about unpaid but not-yet-delinquent taxes is unclear.

Requiring Tenant to pay sales or use taxes "on any and all of the rentals paid by Tenant" is difficult to reconcile with Section 6.3, which bars requiring Tenant to pay "any other tax, assessment, charge or levy upon the Rent payable by Tenant." A court could be asked which section governs a rent tax.

The waiver of any right to cancel, seek diminution of Rent or sue for damages sits against Section 17.2, which expressly lets Tenant cure, offset costs and abate Base, Percentage and Additional Rent on Landlord's default, and against the termination rights in Sections 15.4, 16.2 and 26. A court would have to decide how far the "unless such right is explicitly reserved" carve-out reaches.

The grant of "any lawful purpose, including without limitation" a long enumerated list, followed by a list of prohibited purposes, sets a general permission against enumerated specifics and invites an ejusdem generis or expressio unius reading of the permitted scope. Whether a use outside both lists is permitted, and what "other uses incidental thereto" covers, is left open.

The prohibition on use as "a shooting gallery" is hard to square with Section 23.3, in which Landlord acknowledges Tenant's contemplated "display, sale and demonstration of firearms, smokeless powder, black powder, ammunition." A court could be asked whether an indoor range or firearms demonstration area falls within the prohibition.

A section titled "No Operating Covenant" opens with an affirmative covenant that Tenant "shall open a Gander Mountain store on the Premises within one (1) year after the Delivery Date," and then says no provision imposes obligations respecting operation of the Premises. The duration and enforceability of the opening obligation is left in doubt.

Landlord's recapture notice "must be exercised, if at all, by providing Tenant with written notice following the expiration of such nine (9) month period," fixing no outside deadline, so the right is open-ended in time. Whether "cease for a period in excess of nine (9) consecutive months" is measured net of the listed excluded causes is also unstated.

Permission to use "any portion of the Premises and the Land" for outside display and storage is unbounded and open-ended ("may include, but are not limited to"), with no limit protecting the parking supply the Lease elsewhere measures by ratio in Sections 16.2 and 26.5. How much of the Land may be given over to storage is not stated.

The restriction bites only "to the extent that such sales, in the aggregate, exceed five percent (5%) of its retail sales," leaving "its" ungrounded — the transferee's sales at that property, or company-wide — and giving no measurement period. The trailing clause "and no party has been granted any exclusive use with regard to the Specific Permitted Use" is grammatically detached from the operative prohibition.

The covenant runs only "[f]or so long as the Premises are used for the Specific Excluded Use," yet Section 8.2 lets Tenant cease operations entirely in its sole discretion and Section 8.1 permits any lawful use. A court could be asked whether the radius restriction lapses whenever Tenant stops the outdoor-retail use.

The remedy clause gives damages and injunctive relief without the stipulation, made in Section 3 of the Exhibit D Declaration of Restrictions, that damages are inadequate. A court could be asked whether the availability of damages under this section defeats injunctive relief for the same breach.

"Tenant shall remain fully liable on this Lease" after any transfer is not squared with clause (b)(2), which permits transfer to an entity that "succeeds to the business of Tenant" by merger or asset sale, where the transferor may cease to exist. Whether any assignment can release Tenant is left unstated.

The carve-out relieving Tenant of replacing the parking lot, roof or major building systems in the last three years of the term leaves no one obliged to replace them, since Section 7 provides Landlord need perform no work except as specifically set out. A court could be asked who bears a required roof replacement in that window.

The self-insurance proviso — "provided such self-insurance may not exceed five hundred thousand dollars ($500,000.00)" — has an unclosed parenthesis and does not say whether the cap is per occurrence, per year or in the aggregate. The five-year adjustment to "a CPI index or other benchmark in customary use in the insurance industry" likewise names no determinate standard.

This section permits Tenant to carry the property coverage, including full replacement value coverage on the buildings, "through Tenant's self-insurance" with no cap, while Section 12.1 caps self-insurance for liability at $500,000. A court could be asked whether the building is required to be insured with a carrier at all.

The indemnity reaches any accident "arising directly or indirectly out of the business conducted in the Premises or occurring in, on, or about the Premises," carving out only Landlord's gross negligence or willful misconduct, so it appears to cover Landlord's own ordinary negligence. The qualifier "unless Tenant is compensated therefor by insurance" gives no test for when Tenant is so compensated.

Landlord indemnifies only for its "gross negligence or willful misconduct" and is excused where the damage results from Tenant's negligence, with no rule for concurrent fault. Whether Landlord owes anything where both parties are negligent is left unstated.

Landlord's approval right is confined to components "which adversely affect[] the structural integrity of the Building," a phrase with no stated threshold or method of determination. The following sentence's exception — "except as provided for in this Lease" — does not identify which other provisions restrict Improvements.

The alternative obligation "to otherwise secure the Landlord to its satisfaction promptly upon request" gives Landlord an unbounded discretion that sits against Section 25.12's rule that consents and approvals shall not be unreasonably withheld. What security satisfies Landlord is unmeasurable on the face of the section.

The unqualified duty to "promptly repair and restore" after any casualty must be read against Section 15.4, which lets Tenant terminate and hand the proceeds to Landlord in a late-term casualty, and against Section 15.2's escrow mechanism. Whether restoration is owed pending the Section 15.4 election is unstated.

Payment into "an escrow mutually satisfactory to Landlord and Tenant" is an agreement to agree with no fallback escrow agent or terms if the parties disagree. The section is also silent on how it operates where a fee mortgagee claims the proceeds under Section 18.2.

The absolute bar on surrender, termination and abatement after damage cannot be squared with Section 15.4, which expressly permits Tenant to terminate for a late-term casualty, or with Section 16.2's rent abatement during restoration. A court could be asked which provision governs.

Termination trigger (a) — that "the time necessary to repair or rebuild the Building exceeds sixty (60) days" — is satisfied by almost any material casualty, so the two conditions do not sit as apparent equals. The direction to give notice "to the other" is also a mechanical error, since only Tenant is given the termination right.

The section makes Rent "equitably adjusted" on termination and "equitably apportioned according to the floor space so taken" otherwise, without a formula or decision-maker for what is equitable. It also directs both that Rent "shall abate during the period of restoration" and that it be apportioned by floor space, without saying how the two interact.

The award is given wholly to Landlord "whether such damages shall be awarded as compensation for diminution in value to the leasehold," yet the proviso preserves to Tenant "any other damages allowed Tenant by law," a catch-all that can be read to swallow the grant. Which clause captures a leasehold-value award is contestable.

Default clause (b) — failure to "diligently proceed, after Tenant is aware of same (including by telephonic notice ... to the store manager)" to cure structural maintenance failures — carries no written notice and no fixed cure period, unlike clauses (a) and (c). What counts as awareness and as diligent proceeding is left undefined.

Tenant's remedy of abating Base, Percentage and Additional Rent until a judgment is satisfied cannot easily be squared with Section 4's requirement that Rent be paid "without deduction or setoff for any reason whatsoever" and Section 7's waiver of any diminution of Rent. A court would have to decide whether Section 7's "explicitly reserved" carve-out saves this remedy.

The enumeration is broken: the section runs into a clause "(b)" concerning quiet possession with no preceding "(a)," and then uses "(a)" and "(b)" again for remedies. Which notice period — thirty days or five days — attaches to which default is obscured by the defective drafting.

The declaration that all remedies are cumulative and non-exclusive sits against Section 18.3's exculpation limiting Tenant to Landlord's interest in the Premises and Section 7's waiver of specified remedies. Whether cumulation restores remedies those sections take away is contestable.

The right to enter and "perform any act required of Tenant under any provision of this Lease" is not squared with Section 25.4, which limits Landlord's entry to inspection, showings and Landlord's own repair obligations on twenty-four hours' notice. Whether Landlord may enter to cure is left in doubt.

"Prime Rate" is defined as "the base rate of interest ... established in the Wall Street Journal," but the Journal publishes a prime rate survey rather than establishing a "base rate." Which published figure the parties meant is a question a court could be asked.

Interest at Prime plus two percent on every late amount overlaps the five percent late charge that Section 4.4 fixes as "liquidated damages" for the same lateness. Whether Landlord may collect both on the same overdue installment is unaddressed.

The certifying party must supply "[a]ny other information reasonably requested," an open-ended catch-all after six enumerated specifics, and must certify that all Landlord conditions "have been satisfied (except as stated)." The scope of what may be demanded within fifteen days is not bounded.

Subordination here is "upon the express condition" of nondisturbance, while Section 1 of the Exhibit E form the Tenant must sign subordinates the Lease "at all times ... in all respects" without that condition. Section 25.3 makes the Lease prevail over exhibits, so which controls a mortgagee's demand is contestable.

The promise that "Landlord shall remain fully liable on this Lease" for pre-transfer matters cannot be squared with the following paragraph of the same section, which frees the named Landlord "entirely ... of all obligations of Landlord hereunder" upon sale. A court could be asked which survives a transfer.

The declaration that there is "no personal (or entity) liability of Landlord" and that Tenant may look solely to Landlord's interest in the Premises conflicts with the preceding paragraph of Section 18.3 keeping Landlord "fully liable" for pre-transfer defaults, and with Section 17.2's contemplation of a "final monetary judgment against Landlord." Which limits Tenant's recovery is left open.

Tenant's "absolute right ... without Landlord's further approval" is immediately qualified by requiring Landlord's cooperating documents to be "in a form acceptable to Landlord and Landlord's counsel" and by conditions Landlord "may" impose. Whether Landlord can effectively block a leasehold mortgage through form objections is the resulting ambiguity.

The flat warranty that "Landlord is the fee owner of the Land" is difficult to square with Section 18.3, which defines Landlord to include an owner of "a leasehold interest in the Land (if Landlord's interest is that of a lessee under a ground lease)," and with Section 18.2's subordination to "any ground lessor." Whether a ground lease may exist is left unresolved.

The representation that there are no mortgages or security interests except as set forth in Exhibit G, which lists only two easements, sits against Sections 18.2, 26.1, 6.2.2 and 12.1, all of which assume an existing mortgagee of the fee. A court could be asked whether the representation was breached or merely surplus boilerplate.

The use representation is doubly hedged — "To the knowledge of Landlord" and only "after securing all necessary governmental permits and approvals" — so it may warrant nothing about present zoning or permit availability. Its content sits awkwardly against Section 24.1's unqualified statement that the Premises comply with all existing law.

The covenant of quiet enjoyment is made "subject to the performance by Tenant of the terms and conditions of this Lease," which can be read to forfeit it on any breach however trivial and without regard to the cure periods in Section 17.1. Its interaction with Section 17.2's five-day quiet-possession cure right is not stated.

Tenant must surrender "Improvements made by Tenant (but excluding Tenant's personal property and trade fixtures)," and the Lease nowhere draws the line between Tenant's Work deemed Improvements under Section 5.2 and its removable trade fixtures. The string of casualty and eminent domain exceptions is also drafted so that "casualty damage" appears twice on different conditions.

The definition sweeps in all requirements "otherwise relating to the environment or solid, liquid or hazardous substances," a general catch-all beyond the enumerated federal statutes, with no limit as to future laws. Its outer boundary is left to construction.

"Hazardous Material" extends to anything "regulated as 'hazardous,' 'toxic' or under any other similar designation," an open-ended catch-all, and expressly includes petroleum products and by extension the powder and fuels Tenant sells. Its breadth against Section 23.3's acknowledgment of Tenant's firearms and fuel inventory invites construction.

The first sentence is an unqualified representation that Landlord provided "full, accurate and complete copies" of all environmental reports, while every following warranty in the same section is limited to knowledge "without any independent inquiry or investigation." Which standard applies to the disclosure obligation is contestable.

Tenant covenants against any storage of Hazardous Material "except in strict accordance with all Environmental Laws," while the following acknowledgment says the firearms, powder and fuel operation "does not violate any of the provisions of this Section" on the same condition, so the acknowledgment adds no protection. Whether ordinary retail stock of powder and petroleum products breaches the covenant is left open.

The exclusion for material "placed inside the four walls of the Building or on, in or under the Premises by an invitee or customer of Tenant" is broad enough to strip Landlord's indemnity of most practical content, since almost any on-site material is inside the Premises. Whether the invitee/customer limitation modifies both branches of the exclusion is grammatically unclear.

Tenant's indemnity covers "the introduction onto the Premises of any Hazardous Material by a Tenant Indemnified Person" without limiting the introduction to the Lease term, while Landlord's mirror exclusion in Section 23.4 is expressly limited to "during the term of this Lease." The temporal reach of Tenant's obligation is left unstated.

Tenant must remediate "promptly ... and after Landlord approval," a condition with no time limit or standard for Landlord's approval, which cannot easily be squared with the duty to commence promptly under Environmental Laws. The notice duty is also carved out for "any Hazardous Material which Tenant sells in the ordinary course of business, such as black powder," a category with no boundary.

The unqualified statement that the Premises comply with all existing law as of the Commencement Date sits against Section 5.1, by which Tenant accepts the Building "as is, with all faults and defects ... without representation or warranty." A court could be asked whether the compliance representation survives the as-is acceptance.

The middle of the section is mangled to illegibility ("in | t such laws ... ind ubnot fo, the erection of a fire escape or exit, the same shall be complied with by L ole cost"), so it cannot be read to say who bears the cost of legally required structural changes. The final sentence is also self-contradictory: "At no expense to Landlord, Landlord will cooperate with Tenant."

Binding "successors and assigns" of Landlord cannot be squared with Section 18.3, which frees the named Landlord and any prior owner of all obligations accruing after a sale. Which provision governs a successor landlord's and a predecessor's liability is left to construction.

The rule that the Lease prevails over any exhibit collides with Section 29, which makes the exhibits part of the Lease "with the same force and effect as if set forth in full herein," and with the Exhibit E subordination form whose Section 1 subordinates the Lease unconditionally. A court could be asked whether Exhibit E's terms yield to Section 18.2.

Landlord's entry right is limited to "during Tenant's business hours," but Section 8.2 lets Tenant cease operating entirely in its sole discretion, so there may be no business hours at all. When Landlord may enter a dark store is unaddressed.

The integration clause says the Lease "contains all covenants and agreements between Landlord and Tenant," yet the transaction contemplates separate instruments — the Exhibit D Declaration of Restrictions, the Exhibit E Subordination Agreement and the Exhibit F Memorandum — and Section 26.4 contemplates a later conformed copy. What is inside the integrated writing is contestable.

Notice is "deemed given upon the earlier of personal delivery, the date postmarked, delivery to such courier or the refusal to accept such service," so a mailed notice is effective when postmarked even if never received. Given the one-year non-renewal notices in Sections 3.2 and 3.3 and the cure notices in Section 17, the effect of a lost mailing is a live question.

Extension turns on "circumstances beyond the [party's] control," an undefined standard followed by a non-exhaustive list that includes the counterparty's own "acts," leaving the boundary of excused delay open. The ten-day written notice condition is also stated without saying what happens if notice is late.

The section requires a Memorandum of Lease "in the form attached as Exhibit G," but Exhibit G is the schedule of Permitted Encumbrances and the Memorandum form is Exhibit F. The cross-reference error leaves the form to be recorded in doubt.

The general rule that consents shall not be unreasonably withheld is qualified only by "[e]xcept as expressly provided otherwise," and several sections give a party "sole and absolute discretion" (Sections 5.4, 8.1, 26) while others, like Section 5.5's "location acceptable to Landlord and Tenant," state no standard at all. Which consents this section reaches is contestable.

Landlord's waiver of any lien on Tenant's inventory and equipment sits against Section 22, which lets Landlord "remove and dispose of" Tenant's trade fixtures and personal property at Tenant's expense on surrender. Whether the waiver survives a holdover or default is unstated.

The representation is that there are no other brokerage claims, but the indemnity extends only to "any such claim related to a broker hired by such party," a narrower category that leaves claims by unhired brokers unallocated. The gap between the warranty and the indemnity is on the face of the section.

Holdover Base Rent at "two hundred percent (200%)" is fixed without regard to fault and may be attacked as a penalty, and the section does not say whether Percentage Rent and the Section 4.5 credit continue "upon the same terms and conditions." What accrues during a holdover month is therefore uncertain.

A blanket "time shall be of the essence" cannot easily be squared with the cure periods and diligence standards in Sections 17.1 and 17.2 and with the extensions granted by Section 25.9's force majeure clause. Whether any missed deadline is a material breach is the resulting question.

The offer must be accepted "by April 16, 2004," the very date as of which the Lease is stated to be entered into, so the acceptance window is a single day or already closed. The consequence is also optional and one-sided — the offer "may, at Tenant's sole option, be terminated" — leaving the Lease's effectiveness on late acceptance uncertain.

A termination right exercisable in Tenant's "sole and absolute discretion" after the Contingency Date — which under Section 26.1 can fall on or after the Commencement Date — is hard to square with Section 7's waiver of any right to cancel and Section 5.1's as-is delivery. Whether Tenant may still walk after taking possession is contestable.

The condition that "any party holding a mortgage or other similar interest in the Land has executed a Subordination Agreement" presupposes a mortgagee, while Section 19.3 represents that no mortgages or security interests affect the Land except the Exhibit G easements. Whether the condition is satisfied vacuously or requires an instrument is left open.

The condition requires that "all blanks, bracketed references and incomplete exhibits" be completed, yet the executed instrument leaves Exhibit B a bracketed list of items "[t]o Show" and Exhibit C's dates blank. Whether the failure of this condition gives Tenant a termination right, or the exhibits are simply of no effect, is contestable.

This section conditions Tenant's obligations on a parking ratio of at least 4.2 spaces per 1,000 square feet, while Section 16.2 treats a fall below 3.75 spaces per 1,000 square feet as the trigger for termination after a taking. The Lease thus sets two different adequate-parking standards without reconciling them.

"[M]aterial adverse change in the marketability of the Premises" gives no measure of materiality or of marketability, and the list is garbled by repetition ("the environmental condition of the Premises or the Premises, the condition of the Building and the Premises"). What change permits termination cannot be determined from the words.

Landlord must "use reasonable efforts and diligence to enforce all of the provisions" of easement and operating agreements, a standard the Lease nowhere defines or benchmarks. The prohibition also reaches "any agreements with respect to the Premises," a general phrase whose breadth against the enumerated easement, operation and governmental agreements is contestable.

The waiver reaches "any matters whatsoever arising out of or in any way connected with this Lease, Tenant's use or occupancy of the Premises, and/or any claim of injury or damage," the last limb untethered to the Lease at all. Whether it covers a personal injury or tort claim between the parties unconnected with the Lease is a question of scope.

The metes-and-bounds description contains a broken call — "to a point at its intersection with the division on the west and the property now or formerly owned by said Louis Tokos and Irene Tokos" — omitting the line intended, and the exceptions carve out unspecified "any other property dedicated to the State of New York or the City of Johnson City." The boundary of the Land, and hence the Premises, is therefore not closed by the text.

The Commencement, Delivery and Rent Commencement Dates are left blank in the executed form, so the confirmation Section 2.3 requires supplies none of the dates on which the term and rent turn. Whether the Lease's dates were ever fixed depends on evidence outside the instrument.

The form fixes expiration in "2019," fifteen calendar years from 2004, while Section 2.2 expires the Lease at the end of the fifteenth Lease Year as defined in Section 2.4 and Section 3.3 automatically extends to the following January 31. The printed year and the Lease's own mechanism can produce different expiration dates.

The form describes the options as automatically exercised unless Tenant "presents notice" by stated dates, which are left blank, whereas Section 3.2 fixes the deadline as one year before expiration of the term then in effect. Which statement of the deadline controls is left open.

The recital states that "Landlord owns the parcels" constituting the Restricted Property, while the Declaration is made and the restrictions are undertaken by the "Restricted Party," an affiliate rather than Landlord. Whose land is actually burdened is left in doubt by the recital.

The recital describes the Restricted Party simply as "an affiliate of Landlord," while Section 9.1 of the Lease defines Restricted Parties to include entities controlled by or affiliated with another entity controlled by or affiliated with Landlord. Whether the Declaration reaches the full class Section 9.1 covers is contestable.

The restriction is conditioned on the Premises being "used for the Specific Excluded Use (as defined herein)," but the definition is supplied only at the end of the same sentence and describes uses of the Restricted Property, making the trigger circular. The five percent limb — "to the extent that such sales, in the aggregate, exceed five percent (5%) of its retail sales" — leaves "its" ungrounded and fixes no measuring period.

The list of restricted uses here omits "sale of other casual apparel," which Section 9.1 of the Lease includes in its otherwise identical definition of Specific Excluded Use. Whether the recorded Declaration burdens the same activities the Lease covenant does is therefore contestable.

Termination "on the expiration or termination of the Gander Mountain Lease" sits against Section 1's own condition that the restrictions run only while the Premises are used for the Specific Excluded Use, giving two different end points. Which event releases the Restricted Property first is not stated.

The acknowledgment that "damages are not adequate" cannot be squared with Section 9.2 of the Lease, which gives Tenant a right to damages as well as injunctive relief for breach of the same restrictions. A court could be asked whether Tenant may recover damages for a Declaration breach.

The recital that "Landlord owns the property" is stated flatly, while Section 18.3 of the Lease contemplates that Landlord's interest may be that of a lessee under a ground lease and Section 18.2 contemplates a ground lessor. What estate the Mortgage encumbers is left open by the recital.

The recital equates the whole "Property" with the leased "Premises," while Section 1 of the Memorandum of Lease describes the Premises as lying on "the portion of the property" described in its Exhibit A. Whether the nondisturbance protection covers the entire tract or only part of it turns on this.

The recital states flatly that "Tenant has agreed to subordinate the Lease," whereas Section 18.2 of the Lease makes any subordination conditional on recognition of the Lease and nondisturbance. A party could argue the recital states an unconditional agreement the operative Lease does not give.

Subordination "at all times ... in all respects" without qualification cannot be squared with Section 18.2 of the Lease, which makes subordination expressly conditional on the Lease's validity being recognized and possession undisturbed. Section 25.3, making the Lease prevail over exhibits, sharpens the question of which governs.

Lender's promise that it "will be bound by all of the terms of the Lease" is difficult to square with Section 3(d) of the same agreement, which frees Lender from liability for Landlord defaults, from prior offsets, and from amendments made without its consent. The nondisturbance protection is also made conditional on the opaque proviso "but only provided the terms of this Section are complied with."

The clause ends with a dangling "and (d)" that belongs to the next subsection, so the sentence does not close on its own terms. It also obliges Tenant to take a new lease "containing the same terms and conditions as contained in the Lease" without saying who fixes the new commencement date or the effect of Tenant's refusal.

Subsection (ii) frees Lender from "claims, defenses or offsets ... which arose or existed prior to the time Lender obtains possession," while proviso (B) preserves "any rights of self-help, set-off, abatement or termination expressly provided in the Lease," which is precisely what Section 17.2 provides. The two limbs point in opposite directions on a pre-foreclosure Landlord default.

The Lender cure right operates "[n]otwithstanding any provisions of the Lease to the contrary," overriding the notice and cure scheme of Section 17.2 of the Lease, while Section 25.3 of the Lease says the Lease prevails over any exhibit. Which instrument governs a Tenant termination notice is contestable.

Tenant's direction to pay all rent to Lender on written notice sits against Section 4 of the Lease, which requires Rent to be paid at Landlord's notice address "or at such other place designated in writing by Landlord." Whose direction controls in the event of competing notices is addressed only by this exhibit.

Lender's obligation to make proceeds available is made "subject to such reasonable and customary procedures ... as Lender may impose," while Section 15.2 of the Lease requires the proceeds to be held in an escrow "mutually satisfactory to Landlord and Tenant." Which disbursement regime governs a restoration is left unresolved.

The Lender's notice address is left entirely blank in the form, so the notices this agreement requires — including the Section 4 default notice on which Tenant's right to cancel depends — have no stated destination. Notices are also deemed given on the postmark date rather than on receipt.

The statement that this Agreement "shall not modify or in any way affect Landlord's obligations under the Lease" is hard to reconcile with Section 4, which conditions Tenant's cancellation rights notwithstanding the Lease, and Section 5, which redirects rent away from Landlord. Whether the Agreement alters the Lease bargain is precisely what is in doubt.

Tenant's "absolute right ... without Landlord's or Lender's further approval" is qualified in the next sentence by requiring Lender's documents to be "in a form acceptable to Lender," with no reasonableness standard. Whether Lender can frustrate a leasehold financing through form objections is left open.

An entire-agreement clause superseding "all prior or contemporaneous written ... agreements ... respecting the subject matter" could be read to displace Section 18.2 of the Lease, which sets the conditions on which Tenant agreed to subordinate. Section 25.3 of the Lease says the Lease prevails over exhibits, creating the opposite result.

The description repeats the broken call "to a point at its intersection with the division on the west and the property now or formerly owned by said Louis Tokos and Irene Tokos," omitting the line intended, and excepts unspecified property "dedicated to the State of New York or the City of Johnson City." The Property subject to nondisturbance is therefore not closed by the text.

The recorded Memorandum describes the Premises as lying on "the portion of the property legally described on Exhibit A," without identifying which portion, while the Lease demises the whole Building and Land as the Premises. What the recorded notice puts third parties on notice of is uncertain.

The Memorandum has the initial term expiring "on the fifteenth (15th) anniversary date of the Commencement Date," while Section 2.2 of the Lease expires it on the last day of the fifteenth Lease Year as defined in Section 2.4 and Section 3.3 extends it to the next January 31. The recorded expiration date and the Lease's mechanism can differ by months.

The Memorandum records only that the Premises may be used "for any lawful purpose, subject to certain specific prohibited uses," omitting the exclusivity and Landlord restrictions in Sections 8.1 and 9.1 that Tenant would want of record. What a purchaser is charged with notice of is narrower than the Lease grant.

The Memorandum says it is "executed in accordance with the terms of this Lease" and that "[t]he Lease is deemed to be a material part hereof," using "this Lease" in an instrument that is not the Lease. The mislabeling clouds whether the Memorandum incorporates the Lease of record or merely refers to it.

This copy of the legal description carries the same defective call — "a point at its intersection with the division on the west and the property now or formerly owned by said Louis Tokos and Irene Tokos" — leaving a boundary line unspecified in the recorded instrument. The open-ended exception for property "dedicated to the State of New York or the City of Johnson City" adds further indeterminacy.

Exhibit G is used twice for different purposes: Section 19.3 treats it as the schedule of Permitted Encumbrances, while Section 25.11 requires a Memorandum of Lease "in the form attached as Exhibit G," which is the Exhibit F form. Which document Exhibit G supplies is left in conflict.

The first permitted encumbrance names "Greenwood Builders Supply, Inc.," while the legal description of the Land repeatedly identifies the adjoining owner as "Glenwood Builders Supply, Inc." A court could be asked whether the easement excepted is the one of record.
